questions.q: What posture does this lesson recommend toward incoming review feedback?
options: Treating it like a hypothesis test — checking whether the specific concern raised is valid, rather than defending the design against it regardless of merit
Treating it as a verdict on the design's overall quality to be accepted or resisted as a whole
Ignoring feedback unless it comes from the most senior reviewer in the room
Automatically accepting every piece of feedback without evaluation
questions.explain: The right posture checks each concern on its own merits, like a hypothesis test, rather than treating all feedback as either a devastating verdict or something to be defended against uniformly.

questions.q: What distinguishes "worth discussing" feedback from "must-fix" feedback in this lesson's triage?
options: "Worth discussing" feedback should always be ignored
"Worth discussing" feedback identifies a legitimate tradeoff where reasonable architects could land on either side, while "must-fix" identifies a genuine, previously-missed gap
"Must-fix" feedback is always about cost, never about functionality
There is no real difference between the two categories
questions.explain: Must-fix feedback catches a real gap that needs correcting outright. Worth-discussing feedback surfaces a genuine tradeoff where the feedback isn't wrong, but isn't the only reasonable position either — it warrants a substantive discussion, not an automatic fix or an automatic dismissal.

questions.q: What is the concrete tell this lesson gives for distinguishing "defending the design" from "defending your ego" when responding to feedback?
options: Whether the architect responds politely or rudely
Whether the feedback came from a senior or junior reviewer
Whether the response to feedback changes based on whether the specific concern turns out to be valid, or stays the same regardless of what the concern actually was
Whether the design review happens in person or over email
questions.explain: An architect defending the design on its merits lands in different triage buckets depending on each concern's validity. An architect defending their ego ends up declining everything regardless of merit — a pattern a review board notices and that costs credibility over time.

questions.q: What does "acknowledged-and-declined" mean in this lesson's triage, and how is it different from simply dismissing feedback?
options: It means ignoring the feedback entirely without a response
It is identical to dismissing feedback, just with a nicer name
It means the reviewer's role doesn't entitle them to a response
It means the concern was considered on its merits, the design stands as presented, and the reasoning for declining is stated explicitly on the record
questions.explain: Acknowledged-and-declined finishes the hypothesis test with a recorded answer — the concern was genuinely considered, and the reasoning for standing by the original design is stated explicitly rather than the feedback simply being brushed aside.

questions.q: When a reviewer's pushback seems to stem from "not understanding" the design, what does this lesson say is usually the actual explanation?
options: The gap is usually in how the design was presented (per Lesson 12's structure), not in the reviewer's ability to follow it
The reviewer is usually correct that they don't understand architecture in general
The design itself is always flawed in this situation
This situation never actually occurs in real reviews
questions.explain: Before concluding a reviewer simply didn't understand, this lesson says to re-check the presentation structure from Lesson 12 — in most such cases, the actual gap is in how clearly the problem, alternatives, and design were presented, not in the reviewer's comprehension.
